lessons.title: Receivables, Inventory and Payables: The Balance Sheet Lines Your Department Creates

children.text: Nobody at Kesari Foods ever decided to lock up ₹10 crore. Sales offered distributors 60 days of credit to hit a quarterly target. Procurement bought six months of packaging film to beat a price increase. Production kept extra finished stock so the festive season would not catch anyone short. Each decision was defensible on its own, and together they created a line on the balance sheet larger than the company's annual profit.

These three lines, receivables, inventory and payables, are the part of the balance sheet that managers outside finance actually control. This lesson shows you how your decisions become those numbers, and what it costs.

body.text: Working capital is not a finance item. It is the accumulated residue of operating decisions made by sales, procurement and production, and it is paid for with borrowed money.

children.text: The Three Lines and Who Creates Them

cells: Trade receivables
Sales already made and billed, not yet collected
Credit terms offered by sales, and how hard collections are chased
Cash out of your hands, sitting with customers
Inventories
Raw material, work in progress and finished goods held
Procurement buying policy, production planning, demand forecasts
Cash converted into things on shelves
Trade payables
Purchases received but not yet paid for
Terms negotiated with suppliers, and payment discipline
Cash you are still holding, funded by suppliers

body.caption: Kesari Foods: ₹7 crore + ₹12 crore - ₹9 crore = ₹10 crore locked up

children.text: Receivables and inventory consume cash. Payables supply it. A business that collects fast, holds little stock and pays slowly needs almost no funding. A business that does the opposite has to borrow to stand still, which is why a growing company can be profitable and permanently short of money.

body.label: What ₹10 crore of working capital costs Kesari Foods
body.context: At a cash credit rate of roughly 9.5%, funding ₹10 crore of working capital costs about ₹95 lakh a year in interest. That is close to a fifth of the company's ₹5 crore profit before tax, spent on nothing more than the gap between paying and being paid.

children.text: Measuring It in Days, Not Rupees
Rupee amounts grow with the business, so they tell you little on their own. Convert each line into days and you get a number you can compare across years and against competitors.

body.caption: How long customers take to pay
How long stock sits before it is sold
How long you take to pay suppliers

children.text: Put them together and you get the cash conversion cycle, the number of days your money is out of the business.

body.title: One batch of flour, tracked through the cycle

events.title: Flour arrives at the Indore plant
events.description: The supplier delivers on credit. No cash has moved yet, and trade payables rise.

events.title: The finished snacks are sold
events.description: On average, stock sits for 98 days before it is dispatched to a distributor. Inventory falls, receivables rise.

events.title: The supplier is finally paid
events.description: Cash leaves the company for material bought over four months ago.

events.title: The distributor pays
events.description: Cash finally returns, 88 days after the sale. The company funded the gap between day 126 and day 186 on its cash credit line.

body.text: Kesari Foods pays suppliers in 126 days, and that is not a clever strategy, it is a liability. Under Section 15 of the MSMED Act, 2006, payments to registered micro and small suppliers must be made within the agreed period, which cannot exceed 45 days. Under Section 37(2)(g) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (earlier Section 43B(h) of the Income-tax Act, 1961), amounts still unpaid to such suppliers beyond that limit are not deductible until actually paid, so stretching them raises your tax bill in the same year.

body.title: Calculate receivable days
body.prompt: A Chennai auto components maker reports annual revenue of ₹120 crore and trade receivables of ₹18 crore at year end. What is its DSO, in days?
body.explanation: ₹18 crore ÷ ₹120 crore × 365 = 54.75 days, so customers take close to two months to pay. Against the industry, that may be normal or slow. Against last year's number for the same company, it is a fact you can act on.

body.title: The cycle formula
body.textWithBlank: Cash conversion cycle equals inventory days plus receivable days minus ___ days.
body.explanation: Payables are the one part of the cycle funded by someone else, so they are subtracted. A negative cycle, common in grocery retail, means customers pay before suppliers are paid.

children.text: The Three Levers, and Their Limits
Each line has a lever a manager can pull, and each lever has a cost that shows up somewhere else.
Receivables:

tighten credit terms, grade customers by payment behaviour, invoice on the day of dispatch rather than at month end, chase before the due date rather than after, and use TReDS to discount invoices of large buyers. The limit is commercial. Push too hard and the distributor buys from your competitor.
Inventory:

improve forecasts, buy smaller and more often, clear dead stock even at a discount, and separate fast-moving items from slow ones instead of managing an average. The limit is service. Too little stock means stockouts in the festive quarter, when a lost sale never comes back.
Payables:

negotiate longer terms at the contract stage, pay on the due date and not before, and take early payment discounts only when the implied return beats your borrowing cost. The limit is legal and ethical. Micro and small suppliers have statutory protection, and squeezing a small vendor to fund your own cycle simply moves the problem to a weaker balance sheet.

columns.label: Release working capital
points: Cut 10 receivable days and Kesari frees about ₹1.4 crore
No interest cost, no dilution, no approval needed
Limited by what customers and suppliers will accept

columns.label: Borrow more
points: ₹1.4 crore of extra cash credit at about 9.5%
Costs roughly ₹13 lakh a year in interest, every year
Raises debt to equity and uses up sanctioned limits

body.text: Cutting 10 days of receivables at Kesari Foods releases ₹50 crore ÷ 365 × 10, which is about ₹1.4 crore of permanent cash. That is roughly 28% of the company's annual profit before tax, unlocked without selling a single extra pack.

body.title: Which action shortens the cycle?
body.question: Which of these shortens the cash conversion cycle without hurting customers or suppliers?
options: Paying registered micro suppliers in 90 days instead of 45
Buying three months of packaging in advance to lock in a price
Invoicing on the day of dispatch instead of at the end of the month
Holding extra finished stock ahead of a normal sales month
body.explanation: Invoicing on dispatch starts the credit clock earlier and can pull forward payment by a couple of weeks at no commercial cost. Delaying micro suppliers breaks the MSMED timeline, and the other two options deliberately increase inventory.

body.label: RXIL: Receivables Exchange of India (TReDS)
body.description: One of the RBI-licensed TReDS platforms where MSME suppliers auction invoices drawn on large buyers and get paid early, at a financing cost based on the buyer's credit rather than their own.

body.title: The big customer who wants 90 days
body.scenario: A modern trade chain offers Kesari Foods a ₹15 crore annual order, roughly 30% on top of current sales, but demands 90-day credit against the 60 days distributors currently get. Contribution margin is 48% and the company funds working capital on cash credit at about 9.5%.
body.prompt: Work out whether the deal is worth taking, and what you would negotiate.
body.modelAnswer:
The upside first:
1. Contribution on ₹15 crore at 48% is ₹7.2 crore a year, before any additional fixed costs.
The working capital cost:
2. Receivables tied up = ₹15 crore × 90 ÷ 365 = about ₹3.7 crore of permanently funded balance.
3. Interest on that at 9.5% is about ₹35 lakh a year, which is under 5% of the contribution. On these numbers the credit term alone does not kill the deal.
What actually decides it:
4. Is the volume incremental, or will this chain's cheaper shelf price cannibalise existing distributor sales at full price? Cannibalised volume earns you nothing and costs you the credit.
5. Listing fees, promotional spend and returns on unsold stock, which modern trade contracts usually carry. These sit below gross profit and can consume most of the ₹7.2 crore.
6. Concentration risk. One customer at 30% of sales can dictate terms at every renewal, and a single default now puts ₹3.7 crore at risk.
7. Capacity. If the extra volume triggers a second shift or a new packing line, add those step costs before deciding.
What to negotiate:
8. Ask for 60 days, or 90 days with a 1% early payment discount, which costs far less than the margin you would concede on price.
9. Get the chain onto a TReDS platform so invoices can be discounted at the buyer's credit rating.
10. Cap the exposure with a credit limit, and review it quarterly rather than annually.

children.text: What Finance Watches, and What They Will Ask You

Your finance team tracks these three lines every month, usually in an ageing report that buckets receivables by how overdue they are. When working capital rises, they will come to the department that caused it. These are the questions worth being ready for.

body.caption: Working capital questions by department
headers: The question you will be asked

cells: Sales
Why did receivable days rise this quarter?
Ageing split: how much is beyond 90 days, and with which customers
Procurement
Why did inventory rise faster than sales?
Cover in days by category, and the value of stock not moved in six months
Production
Why is work in progress up?
Batch sizes, changeover times and finished goods held ahead of demand
Finance and treasury
Are we funding growth or funding delay?
Cash conversion cycle this year against last year

children.text: Three details separate a number your CFO will accept from one she will pick apart.
Use averages where the balance swings:
the proper calculation uses the average of opening and closing balances. Year-end numbers can be flattered by a collections push in the last week of March.
Match the numerator to the denominator:
receivable days go against revenue including GST if receivables include GST, which they usually do. Inventory and payable days go against cost of goods sold, not revenue.
Payables should ideally use purchases, not cost of goods sold:
most published statements do not disclose purchases separately, so cost of goods sold is the accepted proxy. Say which one you used.
Consistency matters more than precision. Pick one method, use it for every year and every competitor you compare, and state it on the slide.

body.title: Audit your own working capital
steps: Pull inventories, trade receivables and trade payables for the last two years from your company's balance sheet.
Compute DIO, DSO and DPO for both years using the same method.
Compute the cash conversion cycle and note whether it lengthened or shortened.
Estimate the interest cost of the working capital your company funds, using its borrowing rate.
Ask your finance team for the receivables ageing report and find the amount overdue beyond 90 days.
Check whether any of your suppliers are registered micro or small enterprises, and confirm they are being paid within 45 days.

cards.definition: Inventories plus receivables minus payables: the cash locked in day-to-day operations.
Trade receivables divided by revenue, times 365. How long customers take to pay.
Inventories divided by cost of goods sold, times 365. How long stock sits.
Trade payables divided by cost of goods sold, times 365. How long you take to pay.
Inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days. The days your cash is out of the business.
A schedule bucketing receivables or payables by how long they have been outstanding.
An RBI-licensed platform where MSME suppliers discount invoices drawn on large buyers to get paid early.
Payments to registered micro and small suppliers must be made within the agreed period, capped at 45 days under Section 15 of the MSMED Act, 2006.

points: Working capital is inventories plus receivables minus payables, and it is created by operating decisions, not by finance.
Convert each line into days so the numbers can be compared across years and companies.
The cash conversion cycle is inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days, and it is funded by borrowing.
Releasing days of working capital is free funding. Kesari Foods frees about ₹1.4 crore for every 10 receivable days it cuts.
Stretching payables has legal limits: registered micro and small suppliers must be paid within 45 days, or the expense is disallowed until paid.
Expect to be asked why your department's line moved, so keep the ageing or cover data ready.

body.text: Kesari Foods, the Chennai components maker and the modern trade chain are fictional, and the borrowing rate used is illustrative. MSME payment rules and tax provisions change, so confirm the current position with your finance team before acting on a specific payment decision.
